title: Fast regex in .NET
summary: Construct once and reuse, choose between the interpreter, RegexOptions.Compiled and [GeneratedRegex], write patterns that do less work, and use the allocation-free APIs.

steps.title: Build once, and pick the engine
body: `new Regex(pattern)` parses the pattern and builds a matcher. That is real work, so build each regex **once** and
reuse it (a `static readonly` field, or the generated property below). Building one per request or per line is the
most common regex performance bug in code review. The static helpers (`Regex.IsMatch(input, pattern)`) keep a small
cache, `Regex.CacheSize`, 15 by default: fine for a few patterns, useless once you have more.
Three ways to run the backtracking engine:
- **Interpreter** (the default): cheap to build, slowest to match. Fine for a pattern used a few times.
- **`RegexOptions.Compiled`**: emits IL at run time. Building costs milliseconds and hurts startup; matching is fast.
- **`[GeneratedRegex]`** (.NET 7+): a source generator writes the matcher as C# at **build** time. Compiled speed,
no run-time compile, works with trimming and Native AOT, and you can read and step through the generated code.
The analyzer **SYSLIB1045** flags `new Regex("constant")` that could use it.
```csharp
static partial class Patterns
// C# 13 / .NET 9+: a partial property. On .NET 7 and 8, use a partial method: static partial Regex Slug();
[GeneratedRegex(@"^[a-z0-9]+(?:-[a-z0-9]+)*$", RegexOptions.None, matchTimeoutMilliseconds: 100)]
public static partial Regex Slug { get; }
bool ok = Patterns.Slug.IsMatch("checkout-api");
For a fixed pattern in .NET 7 or later, `[GeneratedRegex]` is the default choice. `NonBacktracking` (previous lesson)
is the choice when you cannot trust the pattern or must guarantee linear time.

steps.prompt: An ASP.NET Core endpoint validates a product slug on every request, with a fixed pattern. Which code belongs in the pull request?
options: A `[GeneratedRegex(..., matchTimeoutMilliseconds: 100)]` static partial property, used by the handler
`Regex.IsMatch(slug, pattern)` and rely on the cache
steps.explain: The generated regex costs nothing at run time to build and matches at compiled speed. `Compiled` inside the handler is the worst option: it generates IL on **every** request. The static helper works but is interpreted and depends on the shared 15-entry cache.

steps.prompt: Match each way of running a regex to its trade-off.
pairs: cheap to build, slowest per match
IL generated at run time: slow to build, fast to match
C# generated at build time: fast, no start-up cost, AOT-friendly
linear time guaranteed, but no lookarounds or backreferences

steps.title: Patterns that do less work
body: The engine is only as fast as the pattern lets it be. Habits that pay off:
- **Negated classes over a lazy dot.** `"[^"]*"` runs straight to the closing quote. `".*?"` stops after each
character to check for a quote, and on a line with a missing quote `.` happily runs past other fields.
- **Anchor** when the match must start at the beginning: `^` lets the engine try one position instead of all.
- **No leading `.*`**: it makes every start position scan the rest of the line.
- **Do not capture what you do not read**: use `(?:...)` or `RegexOptions.ExplicitCapture`.
- **No regex for fixed text**: `Contains`, `StartsWith` and `IndexOf` with `StringComparison.Ordinal` are vectorised
and much faster.
- **Allocation-free APIs** (.NET 7+): `regex.Count(input)`, `regex.EnumerateMatches(input)` (yields `ValueMatch`
structs with `Index` and `Length`, no `Match` objects), and `IsMatch(ReadOnlySpan<char>)`.
And **measure** with BenchmarkDotNet before claiming a speed-up. Below, the negated class keeps each value inside its
own quotes.

regex.text: level=info msg="order placed" user="ana" took="34ms" note=""

steps.title: Quoted values without a lazy dot
prompt: Structured log lines carry `key="value"` pairs. Find every pair, with the named groups `k` (a word) and `v` (the text
Use a negated class for the value: lazy `.*?` and `.+?` are not allowed here.

forbid.message: Uses a negated class instead of a lazy dot

hints: "Anything but a quote" is `[^"]`. Zero or more of them: `[^"]*`.
steps.explain: `[^"]*` cannot cross a quote, so every match stays inside one pair, and the unterminated value finds nothing instead of swallowing the rest of the line.

code: foreach (var m in digits.EnumerateMatches("a1 b22 c333"))
steps.explain: `Count` counts matches without creating `Match` objects. `EnumerateMatches` yields `ValueMatch` structs: only `Index` and `Length`, no groups, no allocations. Slice the input with `AsSpan(m.Index, m.Length)` when you need the text.

steps.explain: The attribute marks a `partial` member, and the generator writes the other half at build time. The containing class must be `partial` too.

steps.title: Review: the slow, wrong quote extractor
prompt: **Symptom.** The audit export is slow on big files, and for the line `id="42" name="Acme, Inc."` it reports one value,
Fix `List<string> QuotedValues(string[] lines)`: every value between double quotes, across all lines, in order.
- Build the `Regex` **once**, before the loop, not once per line.
- Replace the greedy `.*` with a negated class, so each match stays inside one pair of quotes.
template: string[] dojoLines = { "id=\"42\" name=\"Acme, Inc.\"", "note=\"\"", "no quotes here", "msg=\"done\"" };
Dojo.Eq("every value, in order", new List<string> { "42", "Acme, Inc.", "", "done" }, QuotedValues(dojoLines));
Dojo.Eq("no lines, no values", new List<string>(), QuotedValues(new string[0]));

forbid.message: Builds the Regex once, outside the loop

hints: Move `var quoted = new Regex(...)` above the `foreach`.
In a normal C# string a quote is written `\"`, so the pattern `"([^"]*)"` is `"\"([^\"]*)\""`.

steps.title: Sum the bytes without allocating
prompt: A transfer log is one big string with lines like `sent 512 bytes`. Write `long TotalBytes(string log)`: the sum of
every number that is directly followed by ` bytes` (as a whole word: `12 bytesize` does not count, and the number
must not be glued to a letter in front, like `x512`).
Use `regex.EnumerateMatches(log)`: it yields `ValueMatch` structs, so slice the text with
`log.AsSpan(m.Index, m.Length)` and parse it with `long.Parse(span)`. No `Match` objects, no substrings.
A lookahead `(?= bytes\b)` keeps ` bytes` out of the match.
template:
Dojo.Eq("three transfers", 3584L, TotalBytes("sent 512 bytes
sent 1024 bytes
retry 3 times
sent 2048 bytes to 10.0.0.1"));
Dojo.Eq("bytesize does not count", 7L, TotalBytes("12 bytesize, then 7 bytes"));
Dojo.Eq("a number glued to a letter does not count", 0L, TotalBytes("x512 bytes"));
Dojo.Eq("more than int can hold", 5000000000L, TotalBytes("sent 5000000000 bytes"));
hints: Pattern: `\b[0-9]+(?= bytes\b)`. `\b` in front refuses `x512`, the lookahead checks for ` bytes` as a word.
`foreach (var m in amount.EnumerateMatches(log)) total += long.Parse(log.AsSpan(m.Index, m.Length));`
